references.text: The Lord fought for Israel at the Red Sea, and the people stood still while their enemies fled in panic, just as the Midianites fled while Gideon's men held their ground.
At Jericho, the walls fell when the people shouted, and the enemy was defeated through an unusual attack—parallel to how the Midianites were struck down by Gideon's shouts and clamor.
The Philistines turned their swords against each other in confusion, just as the Midianites also turned on one another in panic during Gideon's battle.
The next verse explains how the Lord turned the enemy's sword against them while they fled, serving as a direct continuation of the action described in verse 21.
The psalm explicitly mentions Midian at En-Dor as an example of how God defeated Israel's enemies, a direct reference to Gideon's victory.
The prophet Isaiah refers to 'the day of Midian' as an example of God's mighty victory, pointing back to the triumph of Gideon described here.
